topic: multi-agent planning; privacy leakage; distributed search
status: bounded full-text finding from one sampled ICAPS planning paper
claim: In the audited privacy-preserving planning protocol, replacing private fact names with a shared dummy identifier limits direct disclosure but does not hide whether the represented private-fact group exists/is true during search; privacy claims therefore need an explicit inference threat model, not only message-content labels.
positive_evidence: The paper defines a dummy identifier for one or more true private facts and says other agents can infer the existence and monitor the truth value of a private fact, with possible inference of private actions and causal effects.

The study compares a planner that exchanges search states with planners that exchange additional heuristic information and describes its protocol as preserving privacy more strongly in that comparison.
Performance is quantified separately: on 3,404 single-goal instances, width-1/width-2 success is 77.59%/91.63%, compared with 96.94% for hFF; outcomes vary across domains.
counterevidence: The representation intentionally withholds fact names and can reveal less than protocols that transmit more planning information; it is a meaningful privacy-preserving design, not no protection.
This sampled paper does not claim differential privacy or cryptographic secrecy against all inference, and its stated leakage boundaries are explicit.

sources.sections: MA-STRIPS privacy definition; encrypted state representation; single-goal coverage; conclusion/future work

falsifiable_test: On held-out multi-agent planning tasks, compare raw-state, dummy-fact, and formally protected protocols under a preregistered attacker observing message sequences. Measure goal/plan coverage, communication, and attacker inference AUC for private-fact existence, truth, action identity and causal effects. A privacy claim is robust only if specified leakage stays near chance at an acceptable performance/communication cost.
limitations: One planner family and a bounded set of benchmark domains; no formal differential-privacy guarantee or comprehensive attacker evaluation was audited. The 2023 journal extension was located but not counted as a full-text-reviewed source in this batch.

topic: multi-agent coordination; fairness; efficiency; decentralized execution
status: bounded synthesis of three full-text studies with non-comparable methods and metrics
claim: Improvements in multi-agent systems are conditional on the objective and execution assumptions: a common episode-level signal can expand coordination policies, while fairness mechanisms may trade off throughput in some settings and improve both in others. A gain on one metric does not establish joint improvement in coordination, equity, communication and privacy.
positive_evidence: SIC proves a policy-space result under shared-signal assumptions and reports tested gains in matrix games and predator-prey with 10 seeds for the predator-prey comparisons.
FEN reports 90% utilization/CV 0.17 versus independent agents' 96%/1.57 in job scheduling, but improvements on both measured outcomes in its Matthew-effect and manufacturing simulations.
The privacy-preserving planner reports domain-dependent coverage and explicitly acknowledges residual inference from dummy private facts.
counterevidence: Within its stated testbeds, SIC improves coordination against the reported MARL baselines, and FEN improves both fairness and efficiency in two scenarios; this is not evidence that multi-objective gains are absent.
The formal theorems establish meaningful guarantees within their stated assumptions; the concern is extrapolation across different objectives, channels and settings.

sources.sections: Policy-space theorem; signal design; matrix-game and predator-prey results
Fair-efficient reward; job-scheduling table; Matthew-effect/manufacturing results; seed protocol
Privacy encoding/leakage; domain-dependent coverage and communication

falsifiable_test: Use a common held-out multi-agent resource suite with heterogeneous agents, a declared privacy attacker and controlled signal drop/delay. Compare centralized, independent decentralized, shared-signal, fair-reward and privacy-preserving planning baselines. Report total reward/throughput, minimum per-agent utility and inequality, communication bytes, attacker inference, and robustness across seeds/scales. The conditionality concern weakens if one method improves all outcomes robustly without stronger observability or communication assumptions.
limitations: The three papers use different algorithms, environments, metrics and threat models; their effect sizes cannot be pooled. Two RL studies use small designed environments, and FEN reports five seeds per scenario. This synthesis is not a novelty claim.
